nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
1994 Jan 1. TD Phillips
note: There was no date on the original document so 1994 Jan 1 was assigned since most of the SLHs were prepared from 1994 thru 1997.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Tripletail
Scientific Name: Lobotes surinamensis

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class: Osteichthys
      Order: Perciformes
      Family: Lobotidae

Other Common Names:  bouytender (664), flasher (312 834 869), lumpfish (3121, rockfish
(839), snag-drifter (839), steamboat (869) .

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  A small historic fishery existed in Chesapeake Bay (312). Baughman (839) reports a commercial boat from Apalachicola harvested catches of 600 pounds and 2000 pounds in 1921-1922.

Recreational: Often sought by anglers and considered on of the finest saltwater food fishes (839).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  worldwide in tropical and warm waters (788). In the western Atlantic, from Massachusetts and Bermuda to Argentina (327 788). North of Florida mostly the young drift inshore in the summer (788). Baughrnan (875) reported on specimens from New Jersey.  Found in Mobile Bay in the summer (839), and abundant in the summer off Mississippi (839).

Within Study Area: Found throughout Florida waters.

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: Considered a fish "of sluggish habits? (327). Known to school, possibly for spawning.  A northerly migration or transport with rising temperature has been suggested, with a southerly migration during the fall and winter (870).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Mouths of rivers, passes and bays opening into the Gulf (839), as well as saltwater lagoons in the Pensacola area in summer (839). Also in nearshore, open waters of the Gulf.

Substrate: Found over rocky bottoms in the main ship channel in Tampa Bay (839). Also found in the vicinity of buoys (664) and associated with flotsam in open waters, and around piles and bulkheads in enclosed areas (327). Baughman (839) reported that they are usually found near buoys, beacons, pilings, flotsam, and rock jetties. Close to shore under fallen trees and brush (869). Apparently frequent sand flats at night (833 839). Several authors report that both juveniles and adults are associated with Sargassum (837 867 871 872).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Eggs/Larvae: No information (868).

Juvenile/adults: In Charlotte Harbor, one specimen was collected at 29.8 C (789).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Eggs: No information (868).

Larvae: Individuals 15-25 mm long have been taken in salinities of 10.0 to 19.9% (547) .

Juvenile/adults: The species is apparently indifferent to salinity (839), but Gunter (255) considered they are not found below 20 %. They have been reported from the mouths of freshwater streams (8691, and specimens of about 165 mrn have been taken in nearly fresh water (873 874). In Charlotte Harbor, Wang and Raney (789) collected one specimen at a salinity of 21.3%.

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Broadcast spawner with external fertilization. Oviparous.

Mating/Spawning: Spawning occurs in midsummer in Florida (839). Also reported from July through August in Mississippi (839) and in summer along the Gulf coast (255) . Spawning probably occurs inshore (870). Individuals mature at the age of one (870), with males maturing at the size of 445 mm (870), and females maturing at a size of 455 mm (255).

Fecundity: Fecundity is unknown ( 8 6 8 ) .

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Eggs/Larvae: No information on the eggs is available, and the early larvae are unknown ( 8 6 8 ) .
Juveniles/Adults: Maximum size has been reported as from 106 to 110 mm (788 869). Maximum weight has been variously reported to range from 12.25 kg to 18.6 kg (839) with an average weight between 0.9-6.8 kg ( 8 3 9 ) .

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Feeds on blue crabs (255) and a variety of fish, crustaceans, and barnacles (255 8 3 9). Live sardines, crabs, and shrimp are used as bait by recreational fishermen (8 3 9).
